Singhateh deals with the dense prose he is given well, giving the script as much life and variety as is possible.

Though we understand why the men are aggressive / passive aggressive towards each other, two hours is a long time to spend in a simmering pressure cooker fuelled by a past from which neither man can escape.

Photo by Victoria Wai Unfortunately what was originally a striking twelve minute monologue delivered direct to camera, assumes an altogether more stodgy consistency as a clunkily overwritten play of two meandering hours which at its worst moments, emulate Donald-Trump-at-a-lectern-deviating-from-the-autocue.
Even without one of these Q&As, this is one of the most searing and probing theatre works around.
An intense, thought-provoking play about the seeds of hatred and forgiveness across the apartheid era.
But at two hours, even with an interval, the play is exhausting to sit through, the redeeming features, the performances apart, being how it brings back terrible times...
The set-up promises a powder keg of drama, but the play never quite manages to light it.

Paul Herzberg’s The Moth , which arrives at the Finborough after a lengthy Northern tour in 2025, has the start of something compelling here, but it’s lost in a play that sprawls out in all directions without ever coming into focus.

What works so well as a short monologue does not have the structure to sustain a production of this length, and while there is certainly an important story here, it needs more work to have the same impact on stage.
All of this makes The Moth a promising but clumsy play in the long run — something I doubt it's destined to.
Paul Herzberg’s play expands a monologue into a bloated drama that struggles with repetitive speeches and static character arcs which misses its potential.
What used to be a taut, razor-sharp monologue now feels like a tedious, bogged-down lecture that spends far too much time telling us how to feel instead of just letting the drama breathe.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this expansion of a COVID monologue into a full-length drama about apartheid and forgiveness, with most finding it bloated and repetitive despite its compelling premise and occasional powerful moments.
